claims.claim: Hannah Arendt is characterized as preeminently the theorist of beginnings, whose work reflects deeply on the human capacity to start something new.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Hannah Arendt is preeminently the theorist of beginnings. All her books are tales of the unexpected (whether concerned with the novel horrors of totalitarianism or the new dawn of revolution), and reflections on the human capacity to start something new pervade her thinking.

claims.claim: Arendt emphatically denied that her role as a political thinker involved proposing blueprints for the future or telling people what to do, repudiating the title of political philosopher.
claims.supporting_excerpt: But she emphatically denied that her role as a political thinker was to propose a blueprint for the future or to tell anyone what to do. Repudiating the title of “political philosopher,” she argued that the mistake made by all political philosophers since Plato has been to ignore the fundamental condition of politics

must_not_be_lost: Arendt uses multiple distinctions, often threefold, and employs ancient Greece as an Archimedean point of critique rather than writing conventional political philosophy.
extraction.segment_function: Introduction to the text, identifying Hannah Arendt as a theorist of beginnings, outlining the methodology and structure of The Human Condition, and distinguishing Arendt's project from conventional political philosophy.

claims.claim: The immediate reaction to launching the first man-made satellite into space was relief about escaping imprisonment to the earth, echoing long-standing anticipations found in science fiction and mass desires rather than merely triumphal pride.
qualifications: attended by uncomfortable military and political circumstances
claims.supporting_excerpt: The immediate reaction, expressed on the spur of the moment, was relief about the first “step toward escape from men’s imprisonment to the earth.”

claims.claim: Scientific endeavors aimed at making life artificial and altering human biological characteristics manifest the same underlying desire to escape imprisonment to the earth and reject given human existence.
qualifications: suspected underlying wish to extend life-span
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is the same desire to escape from imprisonment to the earth that is manifest in the attempt to create life in the test tube, in the desire to mix “frozen germ plasm from people of demonstrated ability under the microscope to produce superior human beings” and “to alter [their] size, shape and function”; and the wish to escape the human condition, I suspect, also underlies the hope to extend man’s life-span far beyond the hundred-year limit.

definitions.definition: The very quintessence of the human condition and earthly nature, providing human beings with a unique habitat in which they can move and breathe without effort and without artifice.

distinctions.distinction: The human artifice separates human existence from all mere animal environment, whereas through life itself man remains related to all other living organisms outside this artificial world.
distinctions.item_a: The human artifice of the world

must_not_be_lost: The question of whether to use scientific and technical knowledge to exchange given human existence for a self-made product is a political question of the first order that cannot be left solely to scientists or politicians.
extraction.segment_function: introduces the prologue's central theme of earth-alienation, examining the launching of the first man-made satellite in 1957, the human desire to escape earthly imprisonment, and the scientific drive to transcend given human conditions through artificial life and biological manipulation, framing these developments as fundamental political questions rather than purely scientific ones.

claims.claim: The vita activa is designated by three fundamental human activities: labor, work, and action, each corresponding to a basic condition under which life on earth is given.
claims.supporting_excerpt: With the term vita activa , I propose to designate three fundamental human activities: labor, work, and action. They are fundamental because each corresponds to one of the basic conditions under which life on earth has been given to man.

claims.claim: Action has the closest connection with the human condition of natality because the new beginning inherent in birth is actualized through the newcomer's capacity for action.
claims.supporting_excerpt: However, of the three, action has the closest connection with the human condition of natality; the new beginning inherent in birth can make itself felt in the world only because the newcomer possesses the capacity of beginning something anew, that is, of acting.

definitions.definition: The activity corresponding to the biological process of the human body, bound to vital necessities and having life itself as its human condition.
The activity corresponding to the unnaturalness of human existence, providing an artificial world of things with the human condition of worldliness.
The only activity going on directly between men without intermediaries, corresponding to the human condition of plurality.

distinctions.distinction: Labor corresponds to the biological life process and species survival, whereas work provides an artificial world of durable things distinct from natural surroundings.

extraction.segment_function: definition

claims.claim: The vita activa is always rooted in a world of men and man-made things, and no human life is possible without a world testifying to the presence of other human beings.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The vita activa , human life in so far as it is actively engaged in doing something, is always rooted in a world of men and of man-made things which it never leaves or altogether transcends.

claims.claim: Action is the exclusive prerogative of man and is entirely dependent upon the constant presence of others, whereas labor and work do not strictly require the presence of others in the same way.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Action alone is the exclusive prerogative of man; neither a beast nor a god is capable of it, 1 and only action is entirely dependent upon the constant presence of others.

definitions.definition: Human life in so far as it is actively engaged in doing something, always rooted in a world of men and man-made things.
A second life received upon the rise of the city-state, comprising action (praxis) and speech (lexis) in the realm of human affairs.

distinctions.distinction: The substitution of animal socialis for zōon politikon betrays the loss of the original Greek understanding of politics, conflating the natural companionship of the human species with political organization.
A sharp distinction in a citizen's life between private existence centered in the household and communal existence in the city-state.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between action, which requires the presence of others, and other human activities like labor and fabrication.
The historical significance of translating zōon politikon as animal socialis in obscuring the original Greek understanding of politics.
The opposition between the natural association of the household (oikia) and the political realm of the city-state (polis).
extraction.segment_function: To introduce Chapter II by examining the relationship between human activities and human togetherness, tracing the historical loss of the Greek understanding of politics through the translation of zōon politikon as animal socialis, and contrasting the natural association of the household with the political realm of the polis.

claims.claim: The proposed distinction between labor and work is unusual, lacking support in pre-modern political thought and modern labor theories, yet is supported by the existence of two etymologically unrelated words for these activities in European languages.
qualifications: apart from a few scattered remarks in the history of thought
claims.supporting_excerpt: The distinction between labor and work which I propose is unusual. The phenomenal evidence in its favor is too striking to be ignored, and yet historically it is a fact that apart from a few scattered remarks, which moreover were never developed even in the theories of their authors, there is hardly anything in either the pre-modern tradition of political thought or in the large body of modern labor theories to support it. Against this scarcity of historical evidence, however, stands one very articulate and obstinate testimony, namely, the simple fact that every European language, ancient and modern, contains two etymologically unrelated words for what we have to come to think of as the same activity, and retains them in the face of their persistent synonymous usage.

claims.claim: Contempt for laboring originally arose from a striving for freedom from necessity and impatience with effort that left no permanent monument, later spreading to cover all effort as demands of the polis increased.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Contempt for laboring, originally arising out of a passionate striving for freedom from necessity and a no less passionate impatience with every effort that left no trace, no monument, no great work worthy of remembrance, spread with the increasing demands of polis life upon the time of the citizens and its insistence on their abstention ( skholē ) from all but political activities, until it covered everything that demanded an effort.

definitions.definition: The ancient Greek craftsman, corresponding to the German Handwerker.
A term used later in antiquity to describe artisans, meaning men whose chief interest is their craft and not the market place.

distinctions.distinction: Every European language, ancient and modern, contains two etymologically unrelated words for these activities, and the noun 'labor' never designates the finished product whereas the product itself is invariably derived from the word for work.

must_not_be_lost: The etymological evidence of two unrelated words across European languages for labor and work.
The historical origins of contempt for labor in the ancient Greek polis and shifting classifications of occupations.
extraction.segment_function: introduction to the distinction between labor and work, outlining etymological evidence and historical contempt for labor in ancient thought
unresolved_context: Karl Marx will be criticized in the following chapter.
Benjamin Constant's statement on attacking Rousseau.

claims.claim: The modern historians' opinion that labor and work were despised in antiquity merely because only slaves were engaged in them is a prejudice, as the ancients actually reasoned that slaves were necessary because of the slavish nature of all occupations serving the maintenance of life.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The opinion that labor and work were despised in antiquity because only slaves were engaged in them is a prejudice of modern historians. The ancients reasoned the other way around and felt it necessary to possess slaves because of the slavish nature of all occupations that served the needs for the maintenance of life.

claims.claim: The institution of slavery in antiquity functioned as an attempt to exclude labor from human life rather than as a device for cheap labor or profit exploitation.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The institution of slavery in antiquity, though not in later times, was not a device for cheap labor or an instrument of exploitation for profit but rather the attempt to exclude labor from the conditions of man’s life.

definitions.definition: The human as a member of an animal species characterized by laboring and bodily needs, fully justified in bearing the term animal.

distinctions.distinction: The distinction between the private household inmate as a slave and the household head as a citizen, and between activities hidden in privacy versus those worthy of being seen, heard, and remembered, overshadowed other distinctions in classical antiquity.

must_not_be_lost: Antiquity justified slavery through the slavish nature of labor and necessity, not vice versa.
The modern age elevated labor and the animal laborans while failing to clearly distinguish between animal laborans and homo faber.
extraction.segment_function: Examine ancient and modern views on slavery, necessity, labor, and the vita activa, explaining how antiquity justified slavery through the slavish nature of necessity and how the modern age elevated labor without clearly distinguishing between animal laborans and homo faber.

claims.claim: Smith and Marx both shared a modern contempt for unproductive labor, viewing it as parasitical or a perversion because it does not enrich the world.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Moreover, both Smith and Marx were in agreement with modern public opinion when they despised unproductive labor as parasitical, actually a kind of perversion of labor, as though nothing were worthy of this name which did not enrich the world.

claims.claim: Marx's introduction of the term 'labor power' (Arbeitskraft) was the most original and revolutionary element of his system, as it explains labor's productivity through the production of a surplus beyond its own reproduction.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is because not labor itself but the surplus of human “labor power ” ( Arbeits kraft) explains labor’s productivity that Marx’s introduction of this term, as Engels rightly remarked, constituted the most original and revolutionary element of his whole system.

definitions.definition: A productivity that produces objects only incidentally and is primarily concerned with the means of its own reproduction, capable of producing a surplus beyond what is necessary for its own reproduction.

distinctions.distinction: Unproductive labor was historically despised as parasitical and leaving nothing behind, whereas the modern social viewpoint treats all laboring as productive from the perspective of the life process of mankind.

The productivity of work adds new objects to the human artifice, whereas the productivity of labor power produces objects only incidentally and is primarily concerned with the means of its own reproduction.

must_not_be_lost: The modern age and Marx tended to look upon all labor as work and to speak of animal laborans in terms fitting for homo faber.
Within a completely socialized mankind guided by Marx's ideal, the distinction between labor and work would completely disappear as all things become functions of the life process.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The distinction between labor and work becomes merely a difference in degree if the worldly character, location, function, and length of stay of the produced thing are ignored.
qualifications: conditioned on whether the worldly character of the produced thing is taken into account
claims.supporting_excerpt: It seems that the distinction between labor and work, which our theorists have so obstinately neglected and our languages so stubbornly preserved, indeed becomes merely a difference in degree if the worldly character of the produced thing—its location, function, and length of stay in the world—is not taken into account.

claims.claim: Language and fundamental human experiences teach us that world things are of very different natures and produced by quite different activities, contrasting with subjective human-oriented theories.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is language, and the fundamental human experiences underlying it, rather than theory, that teaches us that the things of the world, among which the vita activa spends itself, are of a very different nature and produced by quite different kinds of activities.

definitions.definition: Things needed by our bodies and produced by laboring that lack stability, appear and disappear for incessant consumption, and are used by life to assure the means of its own survival.
Durable things in the world that are not consumed but used, to which men become accustomed, and which give rise to the familiarity of the world and its customs.

distinctions.distinction: Consumer goods are needed by our bodies, produced by laboring, lack stability, and are incessantly consumed and disappear, whereas use objects belong to an environment of things that are not consumed but used, providing worldly stability and familiarity.

must_not_be_lost: Products of work guarantee permanence and durability necessary for a world.
Products of action and speech depend entirely upon human plurality and must be reified into things to remain in the world.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Things needed for the life process itself possess the least durability among tangible things, as their consumption barely survives production and they decay or perish quickly.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The least durable of tangible things are those needed for the life process itself. Their consumption barely survives the act of their production; in the words of Locke, all those “good things” which are “really useful to the life of man,” to the “necessity of subsisting,” are “generally of short duration, such as—if they are not consumed by use—will decay and perish by themselves.”

claims.claim: Laboring activity differs from working because labor moves endlessly in a recurring circle prescribed by the biological process of the living organism rather than terminating in a finished object.
claims.supporting_excerpt: unlike working , whose end has come when the object is finished, ready to be added to the common world of things, laboring always moves in the same circle, which is prescribed by the biological process of the living organism and the end of its “toil and trouble” comes only with the death of this organism.

definitions.definition: Specifically human life limited by birth and end, following a linear movement full of events that can be told as a story or establish a biography, as distinguished from mere zōē.
Biological life shared with other living things that forever retains the cyclical movement of nature.

distinctions.distinction: bios represents human life as a linear time interval between birth and death full of events and story-making, whereas zōē denotes the biological life and cyclical movement shared with other living things.

must_not_be_lost: Laboring moves in an endlessly repetitive circle prescribed by the biological process of the living organism.
The human world's permanence depends on things more permanent than the activities producing them.
extraction.segment_function: The author analyzes the characteristics of labor, the life process, and the contrast between the cyclical movement of nature and the relative permanence of the human world and human bios.

claims.claim: Marx defined labor as man's metabolism with nature where nature's material is adapted to human wants, indicating a physiological perspective where labor and consumption are stages of the biological life cycle.
claims.supporting_excerpt: When Marx defined labor as “man’s metabolism with nature,” in whose process “nature’s material [is] adapted by a change of form to the wants of man,” so that “labour has incorporated itself with its subject,” he indicated clearly that he was “speaking physiologically” and that labor and consumption are but two stages of the ever-recurring cycle of biological life.

claims.claim: Locke discovered that labor is the source of all property, initiating the rise of labor from a despised position to high esteem.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The sudden, spectacular rise of labor from the lowest, most despised position to the highest rank, as the most esteemed of all human activities, began when Locke discovered that labor is the source of all property.

must_not_be_lost: Marx, Locke, and Smith all equated work with labor, leading to contradictions regarding labor's world-building capacity.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Marx's thought contains a fundamental contradiction regarding labor, viewing it simultaneously as an eternal necessity and defining freedom as liberation from labor.
qualifications: Present in both Capital and early writings
claims.supporting_excerpt: These certainly are minor points if compared with the fundamental contradiction which runs like a red thread through the whole of Marx’s thought, and is present no less in the third volume of Capital than in the writings of the young Marx. Marx’s attitude toward labor, and that is toward the very center of his thought, has never ceased to be equivocal.

claims.claim: Locke had to introduce money as a lasting object so that the perishable output of the laboring body could serve as the basis for property and permanence.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Thus Locke, in order to save labor from its manifest disgrace of producing only “things of short duration,” had to introduce money—a “lasting thing which men may keep without spoiling”—a kind of deus ex machina without which the laboring body, in its obedience to the life process, could never have become the origin of anything so permanent and lasting as property

must_not_be_lost: Marx's contradiction between labor as an eternal necessity and the revolution's goal of emancipating man from labor to enter the realm of freedom.
extraction.segment_function: Examines foundational contradictions and distinctions regarding labor and freedom in the thought of Locke, Smith, and Marx.

claims.claim: The blessing of labor consists of effort and gratification following each other closely so that happiness is a concomitant of the process itself.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The blessing of labor is that effort and gratification follow each other as closely as producing and consuming the means of subsistence, so that happiness is a concomitant of the process itself, just as pleasure is a concomitant of the functioning of a healthy body.

claims.claim: Marx's naturalistic view focused on labor power as a life force capable of creating a surplus, rendering the distinction between work and labor irrelevant to him.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Marx’s consistent naturalism discovered “labor power” as the specifically human mode of the life force which is as capable of creating a “surplus” as nature herself.

extraction.segment_function: An analytical exploration of the blessing of life inherent in labor, the nature of happiness within the biological life cycle, Marx's naturalistic concept of labor power and surplus, and the modern defense of the unhampered pursuit of property and appropriation against the common realm.

claims.claim: The concept of process, common to nineteenth-century sciences, originated from introspection of the biological life process within our bodies, aligning with the activity of labor.
claims.supporting_excerpt: What all these theories in the various sciences—economics, history, biology, geology—have in common is the concept of process, which was virtually unknown prior to the modern age. Since the discovery of processes by the natural sciences had coincided with the discovery of introspection in philosophy, it is only natural that the biological process within ourselves should eventually become the very model of the new concept; within the framework of experiences given to introspection, we know of no other process but the life process within our bodies, and the only activity into which we can translate it and which corresponds to it is labor.

claims.claim: Labor's products and the laboring activity itself remain strictly private, worldless, and incapable of establishing a common world, leading ultimately to worldless hobbies under socialized mankind.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Neither abundance of goods nor the shortening of the time actually spent in laboring are likely to result in the establishment of a common world, and the expropriated animal laborans becomes no less private because he has been deprived of a private place of his own to hide and be protected from the common realm.

definitions.definition: Man conceptualized through the life process and labor, driven by the needs of the body and oblivious of the world to the point of worldlessness.

distinctions.distinction: Homo faber uses his hands and primordial tools freely, whereas animal laborans is driven by bodily needs and does not use the body freely.

must_not_be_lost: The connection between the modern concept of process, introspection, biological life, and labor.
The distinction between animal laborans and homo faber regarding bodily freedom and necessity.
The emergence of worldlessness and private hobbies under socialized mankind.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Division of labor grows directly out of the laboring process and is distinct from the specialization of work.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Division of labor indeed grows directly out of the laboring process and should not be mistaken for the apparently similar principle of specialization which prevails in working processes and with which it is usually equated.

claims.claim: Division of labor presupposes the qualitative equivalence of all single activities requiring no special skill, whereas specialization of work is guided by the finished product requiring different skills.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Yet, while specialization of work is essentially guided by the finished product itself, whose nature it is to require different skills which then are pooled and organized together, division of labor, on the contrary, presupposes the qualitative equivalence of all single activities for which no special skill is required

definitions.definition: A principle growing out of the laboring process that presupposes the qualitative equivalence of all single activities requiring no special skill, representing additive amounts of labor power.
A principle prevailing in working processes that is guided by the finished product and requires different skills which are pooled and organized together.

distinctions.distinction: Division of labor presupposes qualitative equivalence of unskilled activities and relates to the laboring process, whereas specialization of work is guided by finished products requiring diverse skills pooled together in working processes.

must_not_be_lost: Division of labor is rooted in the laboring process, while specialization belongs to working processes.
Mass production relies fundamentally on the replacement of workmen and specialization with laborers and the division of labor.
extraction.segment_function: Examine the distinction between the division of labor and the specialization of work, contrasting laboring processes with work processes and mass production.

claims.claim: The ideals of homo faber—permanence, stability, and durability—have been sacrificed to abundance, the ideal of the animal laborans.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The ideals of homo faber , the fabricator of the world, which are permanence, stability, and durability, have been sacrificed to abundance, the ideal of the animal laborans.

claims.claim: The consumers' society emerged not through the political emancipation of the laboring classes, but through the emancipation of the laboring activity itself.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This society did not come about through the emancipation of the laboring classes but by the emancipation of the laboring activity itself, which preceded by centuries the political emancipation of laborers.

must_not_be_lost: Transformation of the work process by the division of labor turning work into labor.
Levelling of all human activities to the common denominator of making a living.
extraction.segment_function: Examines the triumph of the animal laborans, the transformation of work into labor through the division of labor and mass consumption, and the emergence of a consumers' society where all activities are leveled to the standard of making a living.

claims.claim: The danger of future automation is that human productivity will be consumed by an intensified biological life process rather than simply mechanizing natural life.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The danger of future automation is less the much deplored mechanization and artificialization of natural life than that, its artificiality notwithstanding, all human productivity would be sucked into an enormously intensified life process and would follow automatically, without pain or effort, its ever-recurrent natural cycle.

claims.claim: Universal unhappiness in modern society stems from a labor society that lacks sufficient laboring to maintain the balance required for animal laborans happiness.
qualifications: only the animal laborans demands happiness
claims.supporting_excerpt: The universal demand for happiness and the widespread unhappiness in our society (and these are but two sides of the same coin) are among the most persuasive signs that we have begun to live in a labor society which lacks enough laboring to keep it contented.

extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The modern economy has increasingly become a waste economy characterized by the rapid consumption and discarding of goods to keep economic processes going.
claims.supporting_excerpt: One of the obvious danger signs that we may be on our way to bring into existence the ideal of the animal laborans is the extent to which our whole economy has become a waste economy, in which things must be almost as quickly devoured and discarded as they have appeared in the world, if the process itself is not to come to a sudden catastrophic end.

claims.claim: The human world consists of things that are used rather than consumed, and these durable things provide the condition that enables human life to be at home on earth.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The world, the man-made home erected on earth and made of the material which earthly nature delivers into human hands, consists not of things that are consumed but of things that are used. If nature and the earth generally constitute the condition of human life , then the world and the things of the world constitute the condition under which this specifically human life can be at home on earth.

definitions.definition: The man-made home erected on earth, consisting of things that are used rather than consumed, whose permanence stands in contrast to biological life.

distinctions.distinction: Nature constitutes the general condition of human life and provides materials, whereas the world and its things constitute the condition under which specifically human life can be at home on earth through durability and use.

extraction.segment_function: conclusion

claims.claim: The work of our hands (homo faber) fabricates the human artifice out of things whose durability and objectivity provide stability and shelter for mortal human life.
qualifications: distinguished from the labor of our bodies and animal laborans
claims.supporting_excerpt: The work of our hands, as distinguished from the labor of our bodies— homo faber who makes and literally “works upon” 1 as distinguished from the animal laborans which labors and “mixes with”—fabricates the sheer unending variety of things whose sum total constitutes the human artifice.

claims.claim: Although use involves a wearing-out process through contact with a living organism, destruction is incidental to use rather than inherent to it in the manner of consumption.
qualifications: destruction is incidental to use but inherent in consumption
claims.supporting_excerpt: What distinguishes the most flimsy pair of shoes from mere consumer goods is that they do not spoil if I do not wear them, that they have an independence of their own, however modest, which enables them to survive even for a considerable time the changing moods of their owner.

definitions.definition: The sum total of the unending variety of things made and fabricated by homo faber, mostly objects for use that provide stability and solidity for human life.
The relative independence and endurance of world things that allow them to withstand the voracious needs and wants of their living makers and users, enabling humans to retrieve their identity.

distinctions.distinction: Work is performed by homo faber who makes and works upon things to create the human artifice, whereas labor is performed by the animal laborans which mixes with things.
Destruction is incidental to use and wears down durability, whereas destruction is the inherent end and destiny of all things for consumption.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between homo faber and animal laborans
The role of durability and objectivity in stabilizing human life against nature and consumption
extraction.segment_function: Define the concept of work, the human artifice, and the durability and objectivity of world things as distinguished from labor and consumption.

claims.claim: Fabrication consists in reification, where materials are taken from nature through an act of violation and violence, making homo faber a destroyer of nature.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Fabrication, the work of homo faber , consists in reification. Solidity, inherent in all, even the most fragile, things, comes from the material worked upon, but this material itself is not simply given and there, like the fruits of field and trees which we may gather or leave alone without changing the household of nature. Material is already a product of human hands which have removed it from its natural location, either killing a life process, as in the case of the tree which must be destroyed in order to provide wood, or interrupting one of nature’s slower processes, as in the case of iron, stone, or marble torn out of the womb of the earth. This element of violation and violence is present in all fabrication, and homo faber , the creator of the human artifice, has always been a destroyer of nature.

claims.claim: The experience of violence in fabrication is the most elemental experience of human strength, providing self-assurance and satisfaction distinct from the pleasure of labor.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The experience of this violence is the most elemental experience of human strength and, therefore, the very opposite of the painful, exhausting effort experienced in sheer labor. It can provide self-assurance and satisfaction, and can even become a source of self-confidence throughout life, all of which are quite different from the bliss which can attend a life spent in labor and toil or from the fleeting, though intense pleasure of laboring itself

definitions.definition: The work of homo faber that consists in reification and involves the violation and destruction of nature to build the human artifice.
A process realized in fabrication where materials are transformed and secured, contrasted with agricultural tilling which must be perpetually repeated.

distinctions.distinction: The animal laborans remains the servant of nature and the earth, whereas homo faber conducts himself as lord and master of the whole earth through acts of fabrication and destruction of nature.

extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The work of fabrication is guided by a model, such as a mental image or blueprint, which precedes the actual work process and exists outside the fabricator.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The actual work of fabrication is performed under the guidance of a model in accordance with which the object is constructed. This model can be an image beheld by the eye of the mind or a blueprint in which the image has already found a tentative materialization through work. In either case, what guides the work of fabrication is outside the fabricator and precedes the actual work process in much the same way as the urgencies of the life process within the laborer precede the actual labor process.

claims.claim: The process of making is entirely determined by the categories of means and end, where the fabricated thing serves as an independent enduring end product.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The process of making is itself entirely determined by the categories of means and end. The fabricated thing is an end product in the twofold sense that the production process comes to an end in it (“the process disappears in the product,” as Marx said) and that it is only a means to produce this end.

distinctions.distinction: Multiplication multiplies something that already possesses a relatively stable, relatively permanent existence in the world, whereas repetition is urged upon and remains subject to the biological cycle.

extraction.segment_function: Examine the role of models, multiplication, and means-end categories in the process of fabrication within the vita activa.

claims.claim: The continuous automatic process of manufacturing has replaced human standards of utility or beauty with shapes primarily determined by machine operation.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In place of both utility and beauty, which are standards of the world, we have come to design products that still fulfil certain “basic functions” but whose shape will be primarily determined by the operation of the machine.

claims.claim: For a society of laborers, the world of machines acts as a substitute for the real world, despite failing to provide the permanence and stability of the human artifice.
claims.supporting_excerpt: For a society of laborers, the world of machines has become a substitute for the real world, even though this pseudo world cannot fulfil the most important task of the human artifice, which is to offer mortals a dwelling place more permanent and more stable than themselves.

extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Consistent utilitarianism suffers from an innate incapacity to distinguish between utility and meaningfulness, trapping itself in an unending chain of means and ends.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This perplexity, inherent in all consistent utilitarianism, the philosophy of homo faber par excellence, can be diagnosed theoretically as an innate incapacity to understand the distinction between utility and meaningfulness, which we express linguistically by distinguishing between “in order to” and “for the sake of.”

claims.claim: Kant's anthropocentric formulation that human beings are ends in themselves attempts to stop the unending chain of means and ends, yet still originates in utilitarian thinking and leads to treating nature and the world as mere means.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The anthropocentric utilitarianism of homo faber has found its greatest expression in the Kantian formula that no man must ever become a means to an end, that every human being is an end in himself.

definitions.definition: The fabricator who thinks entirely in terms of means and ends arising directly out of work activity.

distinctions.distinction: Expressed linguistically by distinguishing between 'in order to' (utility) and 'for the sake of' (meaningfulness).

must_not_be_lost: Utility established as meaning generates meaninglessness.
Homo faber is incapable of understanding meaning just as animal laborans is incapable of understanding instrumentality.
extraction.segment_function: Diagnosing the perplexity of utilitarianism and the meaninglessness generated when utility is established as meaning within the framework of homo faber.

claims.claim: The instrumentalization inherent in homo faber implies a degradation of all things into means, stripping objects, nature, and the earth of their intrinsic and independent value because they lack reification from work.
qualifications: applies to man in so far as he is homo faber
claims.supporting_excerpt: Man, in so far as he is homo faber , instrumentalizes, and his instrumentalization implies a degradation of all things into means, their loss of intrinsic and independent value, so that eventually not only the objects of fabrication but also “the earth in general and all forces of nature,” which clearly came into being without the help of man and have an existence independent of the human world, lose their “value because [they] do not present the reification which comes from work.”

claims.claim: The Greek classical period declared arts and crafts to be banausic or philistine because work with instruments was done for the sake of producing something else rather than for its own sake, reflecting vulgarity in expediency.
qualifications: limited to the Greeks in their classical period
claims.supporting_excerpt: It was for no other reason than this attitude of homo faber to the world that the Greeks in their classical period declared the whole field of the arts and crafts, where men work with instruments and do something not for its own sake but in order to produce something else, to be banausic , a term perhaps best translated by “philistine,” implying vulgarity of thinking and acting in terms of expediency.

definitions.definition: A term best translated by 'philistine,' implying vulgarity of thinking and acting in terms of expediency, applied by the classical Greeks to the field of arts and crafts where men work with instruments to produce something else.

distinctions.distinction: Fabrication treats the finished product as an end in itself, whereas when the life process takes hold of things for its purposes and the standards of homo faber rule unconditionally, instrumentality changes into limitless instrumentalization.
distinctions.item_a: instrumentality as a limited, productive process in fabrication
distinctions.item_b: limitless instrumentalization driven by the life process taking hold of things

must_not_be_lost: Plato's argument against Protagoras regarding 'man is the measure of all use things (chrēmata)'
Plato's counter-formula that 'the god is the measure [even] of mere use objects' to combat the devaluation of world and nature.
extraction.segment_function: Analyzing how homo faber's instrumentalization of nature leads to the degradation of things into means, the Greek contempt for banausic/utilitarian attitudes, the generalization of the fabrication experience, and Plato's critique of Protagoras's measure formula in favor of the divine standard.

claims.claim: Value is exclusively acquired in the public realm through appearance and esteem rather than by labor, work, capital, profit, or material.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This value consists solely in the esteem of the public realm where the things appear as commodities, and it is neither labor, nor work, nor capital, nor profit, nor material, which bestows such value upon an object, but only and exclusively the public realm where it appears to be esteemed, demanded, or neglected.

claims.claim: Universal relativity and the loss of intrinsic worth are inherent properties of the concept of value itself in the exchange market.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Universal relativity, that a thing exists only in relation to other things, and loss of intrinsic worth, that nothing any longer possesses an “objective” value independent of the ever-changing estimations of supply and demand, are inherent in the very concept of value itself.

definitions.definition: The quality a thing acquires automatically the moment it appears in public as a commodity in the exchange market, consisting solely in public esteem.
An objective quality of a thing itself, attached to the thing, existing outside the will of the individual purchaser or seller, and unchanging unless the thing itself changes.

distinctions.distinction: Marketable value is altered by the change of proportion a commodity bears to something else in the exchange market, whereas intrinsic worth is an objective quality attached to the thing itself that can only be changed through the physical alteration of the thing.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between use value and exchange value
Marx's view on value and socialist distribution
Homo faber's inability to bear the loss of absolute standards
extraction.segment_function: Examine the distinction between intrinsic worth and exchange value, explaining how things become values through the public exchange market and how this produces universal relativity.

claims.claim: Works of art possess a durability of a higher order and are untouched by natural processes of use, which would destroy them rather than actualize their purpose.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Because of their outstanding permanence, works of art are the most intensely worldly of all tangible things; their durability is almost untouched by the corroding effect of natural processes, since they are not subject to the use of living creatures, a use which, indeed, far from actualizing their own inherent purpose—as the purpose of a chair is actualized when it is sat upon—can only destroy them.

claims.claim: The immediate source of the art work is the human capacity for thought.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The immediate source of the art work is the human capacity for thought, as man’s “propensity to truck and barter” is the source of exchange objects, and as his ability to use is the source of use things.

must_not_be_lost: Works of art are strictly without utility and unique, defying equalization through money.
Thought transforms mute feelings and allows them to be reified into the world.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The stability of the man-made human artifice as a home for mortals depends on its transcending both the functionalism of consumption and the utility of use.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The man-made world of things, the human artifice erected by homo faber , becomes a home for mortal men, whose stability will endure and outlast the ever-changing movement of their lives and actions, only insomuch as it transcends both the sheer functionalism of things produced for consumption and the sheer utility of objects produced for use.

claims.claim: Acting and speaking men require the help of artists, poets, historiographers, and writers so that the stories they enact and tell can survive.
claims.supporting_excerpt: If the animal laborans needs the help of homo faber to ease his labor and remove his pain, and if mortals need his help to erect a home on earth, acting and speaking men need the help of homo faber in his highest capacity, that is, the help of the artist, of poets and historiographers, of monument-builders or writers, because without them the only product of their activity, the story they enact and tell, would not survive at all.

must_not_be_lost: The human artifice must transcend functionalism and utility to serve as a stable home.
Action and speech are inherently futile and leave no material product without the help of artists and writers.
The measure of things can be neither the necessity of biological life nor utilitarian instrumentalism.
extraction.segment_function: Conclude the discussion of the human artifice, action, speech, and the measure of things.

claims.claim: Human plurality has a twofold character of equality and distinction, where equality enables mutual understanding and planning, and distinction necessitates speech and action for communication.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Human plurality, the basic condition of both action and speech, has the twofold character of equality and distinction. If men were not equal, they could neither understand each other and those who came before them nor plan for the future and foresee the needs of those who will come after them. If men were not distinct, each human being distinguished from any other who is, was, or will ever be, they would need neither speech nor action to make themselves understood.

claims.claim: To act means to take an initiative or begin something new, reflecting the human condition of natality where men as newcomers initiate action out of freedom.
claims.supporting_excerpt: To act, in its most general sense, means to take an initiative, to begin (as the Greek word archein , “to begin,” “to lead,” and eventually “to rule,” indicates), to set something into motion (which is the original meaning of the Latin agere ). Because they are initium , newcomers and beginners by virtue of birth, men take initiative, are prompted into action.

definitions.definition: The curious quality of alteritas possessed by everything that is, transcending every particular quality and found in its most abstract form in the sheer multiplication of inorganic objects.
An activity involving word and deed by which humans insert themselves into the human world, taking an initiative and beginning something new.

distinctions.distinction: Otherness is shared with everything that is, whereas distinctness is shared with everything alive, and in man both become uniqueness in human plurality.
Equality allows men to understand each other and plan for the future, while distinction makes speech and action necessary for mutual understanding beyond basic needs.

must_not_be_lost: Human plurality combines equality and distinction.
Speech and action reveal unique distinctness and insert humans into the world as a second birth.
Action is rooted in natality as initium (beginning).
extraction.segment_function: Explaining the conditions of human plurality, distinctness, speech, action, and natality as the foundation of the vita activa.

claims.claim: The revelatory quality of speech and action emerges in sheer human togetherness where people are neither for nor against each other.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This revelatory quality of speech and action comes to the fore where people are with others and neither for nor against them—that is, in sheer human togetherness.

claims.claim: Attempting to verbalize who someone is inevitably leads to describing what they are in terms of shared qualities, causing their specific uniqueness to escape.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The moment we want to say who somebody is, our very vocabulary leads us astray into saying what he is; we get entangled in a description of qualities he necessarily shares with others like him; we begin to describe a type or a “character” in the old meaning of the word, with the result that his specific uniqueness escapes us.

must_not_be_lost: Action requires the public realm and the disclosure of the agent ('who') rather than merely the achievement ('what').
Human affairs inherently lack the stability and tangibility of things because they are driven by the unreliable manifestations of acting and speaking beings.
extraction.segment_function: The block explains how speech and action reveal the unique identity of the agent within human togetherness and why action loses this revelatory quality when reduced to a means-end activity.

claims.claim: Greek and Latin languages contain two interrelated pairs of words for 'to act'—archein and prattein, and agere and gerere—originally reflecting a division between the beginning made by a single person and the achievement accomplished by many.
qualifications: distinguishes ancient languages from modern languages
claims.supporting_excerpt: In order to illustrate what is at stake here we may remember that Greek and Latin, unlike the modern languages, contain two altogether different and yet interrelated words with which to designate the verb “to act.” To the two Greek verbs archein (“to begin,” “to lead,” finally “to rule”) and prattein (“to pass through,” “to achieve,” “to finish”) correspond the two Latin verbs agere (“to set into motion,” “to lead”) and gerere (whose original meaning is “to bear”).

claims.claim: Because the actor always moves in relation to other acting beings, doing and suffering are inseparable sides of the same coin, and the consequences of action are inherently boundless because every reaction operates as a new action that triggers chain reactions.
qualifications: applies universally to human action regardless of the scale of circumstances
claims.supporting_excerpt: Because the actor always moves among and in relation to other acting beings, he is never merely a “doer” but always and at the same time a sufferer. To do and to suffer are like opposite sides of the same coin, and the story that an act starts is composed of its consequent deeds and sufferings. These consequences are boundless, because action, though it may proceed from nowhere, so to speak, acts into a medium where every reaction becomes a chain reaction and where every process is the cause of new processes.

definitions.definition: A Greek verb meaning 'to begin,' 'to lead,' and eventually 'to rule.'
A Greek verb meaning 'to pass through,' 'to achieve,' or 'to finish,' which became the accepted word for action in general.
A Latin verb meaning 'to set into motion' or 'to lead.'
A Latin verb meaning 'to bear,' which became an accepted word for action in general.

distinctions.distinction: The original interdependent role of the beginner and leader who depended upon others shifted into the function of a ruler who commands, is isolated, and monopolizes the achievements of others.
They are like opposite sides of the same coin, representing the actor as both a doer and concurrently someone who suffers the consequences in relation to other acting beings.

must_not_be_lost: The etymological shift in terms for action from beginnings to rule.
The boundlessness and chain-reaction nature of human action.
The inherent frailty of human institutions and laws arising from natality.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze the etymological roots, boundlessness, unpredictability, and relational nature of action, highlighting the historical shift from interdependent leadership to solitary rule, and examining how action inherently transcends limitations and threatens human institutions.

claims.claim: The Greek agonal spirit prioritized individual self-disclosure and measured up against others, remaining relatively untouched by the unpredictability of action.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It stresses the urge toward self-disclosure at the expense of all other factors and therefore remains relatively untouched by the predicament of unpredictability. As such it became the prototype of action for Greek antiquity and influenced, in the form of the so-called agonal spirit, the passionate drive to show one’s self in measuring up against others that underlies the concept of politics prevalent in the city-states.

claims.claim: The Greeks treated legislation as a prepolitical act of making rather than a political activity, comparing the lawmaker to a builder or architect who created the framework before politics could begin.
claims.supporting_excerpt: An outstanding symptom of this prevailing influence is that the Greeks, in distinction from all later developments, did not count legislating among the political activities. In their opinion, the lawmaker was like the builder of the city wall, someone who had to do and finish his work before political activity could begin.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between action (praxis) and making (poiēsis) in Greek thought
Legislation as a prepolitical activity of making for the Greeks
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The polis is defined as the organization of people arising from acting and speaking together, with its true space lying between people living together for this purpose rather than its physical location.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The polis , properly speaking, is not the city-state in its physical location; it is the organization of the people as it arises out of acting and speaking together, and its true space lies between people living together for this purpose, no matter where they happen to be.

claims.claim: Power springs up between people when they act together and vanishes the moment they disperse, remaining distinct from the natural quality of individual strength.
claims.supporting_excerpt: While strength is the natural quality of an individual seen in isolation, power springs up between men when they act together and vanishes the moment they disperse.

definitions.definition: The organization of the people as it arises out of acting and speaking together, whose true space lies between people living together for this purpose regardless of physical location.
The space where I appear to others as others appear to me, where men make their appearance explicitly, coming into being wherever men are together in the manner of speech and action.
A power potential that springs up between men when they act together, exists only in its actualization, and keeps the public realm in existence.
The natural quality of an individual seen in isolation.

distinctions.distinction: Strength is the natural quality of an individual seen in isolation, whereas power springs up between men when they act together and vanishes the moment they disperse.
Power cannot be stored up and kept in reserve for emergencies like the instruments of violence, but exists only in its actualization.

must_not_be_lost: The spatial and relational nature of the polis and the space of appearance.
The conceptual distinction between power (as potential actualized in word and deed) and individual strength or stored instruments of violence.
extraction.segment_function: definition

claims.claim: The ancient estimation of politics rests on the conviction that individuals appear and confirm themselves in unique distinctness through speech and action.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The root of the ancient estimation of politics is the conviction that man qua man, each individual in his unique distinctness, appears and confirms himself in speech and action, and that these activi ties, despite their material futility, possess an enduring quality of their own because they create their own remembrance.

claims.claim: Both homo faber and animal laborans are strictly unpolitical because they judge public activities in terms of usefulness to higher ends rather than value appearance and actualization.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Both, therefore, are, strictly speaking, unpolitical, and will incline to denounce action and speech as idleness, idle busybodyness and idle talk, and generally will judge public activities in terms of their usefulness to supposedly higher ends

definitions.definition: The one sense that fits our five strictly individual senses and their particular data into reality as a whole, allowing us to recognize them as disclosures of reality.

distinctions.distinction: Homo faber views public activities in terms of making the world more useful and beautiful, whereas animal laborans views them in terms of making life easier and longer.

extraction.segment_function: The author examines the political standing of speech and action relative to homo faber and animal laborans, the role of common sense, and the distinct forms of alienation found in commercial and laboring societies.

claims.claim: The calamities of action arise from the human condition of plurality, which constitutes the space of appearance in the public realm.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The calamities of action all arise from the human condition of plurality, which is the condition sine qua non for that space of appearance which is the public realm.

claims.claim: The traditional escape from the frailty of human affairs into rule rests on a deep suspicion of action and a desire to find a substitute for it.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The commonplace notion already to be found in Plato and Aristotle that every political community consists of those who rule and those who are ruled (on which assumption in turn are based the current definitions of forms of government—rule by one or monarchy, rule by few or oligarchy, rule by many or democracy) rests on a suspicion of action rather than on a contempt for men, and arose from the earnest desire to find a substitute for action rather than from any irresponsible or tyrannical will to power.

definitions.definition: The human condition that serves as the condition sine qua non for the space of appearance which is the public realm, and from which the calamities of action arise.

distinctions.distinction: Plato opened a gulf between these two modes of action, which according to Greek understanding were originally interconnected, by dividing the beginner (ruler) from those who execute orders.

extraction.segment_function: Examines the historical and philosophical tendency to escape the uncertainties of human action by substituting rule and making, tracing this movement from ancient tyranny to Plato's political philosophy.

claims.claim: The action process is never exhausted by a single deed and possesses an endurance superior to man-made products, but it burdens human beings with irreversibility and unpredictability.
qualifications: dependent on the ability to bear the burden of irreversibility and unpredictability
claims.supporting_excerpt: That deeds possess such an enormous capacity for endurance, superior to every other man-made product, could be a matter of pride if men were able to bear its burden, the burden of irreversibility and unpredictability, from which the action process draws its very strength.

claims.claim: Western philosophical and political tradition wrongly identifies sovereignty with freedom, viewing action negatively because sovereignty contradicts the condition of human plurality.
qualifications: applies to political and philosophic thought throughout the Western tradition
claims.supporting_excerpt: their basic error seems to lie in that identification of sovereignty with freedom which has always been taken for granted by political as well as philosophic thought. If it were true that sovereignty and freedom are the same, then indeed no man could be free, because sovereignty, the ideal of uncompromising self-sufficiency and mastership, is contradictory to the very condition of plurality.

must_not_be_lost: Identification of sovereignty with freedom is an error because sovereignty contradicts plurality.
Action processes are irreversible, unpredictable, and enduring.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The moral code inferred from the faculties of forgiving and promising rests entirely on experiences grounded in the presence of others, unlike the Platonic notion of rule which is derived from a self-relationship.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The moral code, on the other hand, inferred from the faculties of forgiving and of making promises, rests on experiences which nobody could ever have with himself, which, on the contrary, are entirely based on the presence of others.

claims.claim: Jesus of Nazareth discovered the role of forgiveness in human affairs, a discovery whose religious articulation does not diminish its strictly secular political significance.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The discoverer of the role of forgiveness in the realm of human affairs was Jesus of Nazareth. The fact that he made this discovery in a religious context and articulated it in religious language is no reason to take it any less seriously in a strictly secular sense.

distinctions.distinction: Platonic rulership draws its guiding principles from self-domination and a relationship established between oneself and oneself, whereas the moral code of forgiving and promising rests entirely on experiences based on the presence of others.
distinctions.item_b: Moral code inferred from forgiving and promising

must_not_be_lost: Forgiving and promising provide necessary remedies and corrective limits to the irreversibility and unpredictability of human action.
Applying action's processes into the natural realm or acting strictly in the mode of fabrication without action's remedies risks destroying the conditions of human life.
extraction.segment_function: Discuss the moral standards of action based on forgiving and promising, contrasting them with Platonic rule, examining the dangers of applying action without its remedies to nature or fabrication, and tracing the secular political significance of Jesus of Nazareth's discovery of forgiveness.

claims.claim: Three great events stand at the threshold of the modern age and determine its character: the discovery of America and the exploration of the earth, the Reformation's expropriation and social wealth accumulation, and the invention of the telescope with a new universe-viewing science.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Three great events stand at the threshold of the modern age and determine its character: the discovery of America and the ensuing exploration of the whole earth; the Reformation, which by expropriating ecclesiastical and monastic possessions started the twofold process of individual expropriation and the accumulation of social wealth; the invention of the telescope and the development of a new science that considers the nature of the earth from the viewpoint of the universe.

claims.claim: The precursors associated with these three great events were not revolutionists, and their motives and intentions remained rooted in tradition.
claims.supporting_excerpt: These precursors are not revolutionists, and their motives and intentions are still securely rooted in tradition.

must_not_be_lost: Three great events determining the modern age: discovery of the earth, Reformation expropriation and wealth accumulation, invention of the telescope/new science.
The precursors of the modern age were not revolutionists and remained rooted in tradition.
extraction.segment_function: Introducing the modern age and world alienation through three foundational historical events: the discovery of the earth, the Reformation's wealth accumulation and expropriation, and the rise of modern science, alongside the subsequent shrinkage of the globe through speed.

claims.claim: Galileo's use of the telescope and his demonstration of the laws of falling bodies set the stage for a new world view that amalgamated terrestrial and heavenly bodies under the same exterior force.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Except for the numerically small, politically inconsequential milieu of learned men—astronomers, philosophers, and theologians—the telescope created no great excitement; public attention was drawn, rather, to Galileo’s dramatic demonstration of the laws of falling bodies, taken to be the beginning of modern natural science

claims.claim: Galileo achieved what philosophers and astronomers could not by using the telescope to deliver the secrets of the universe to human cognition with the certainty of sense-perception.
claims.supporting_excerpt: What Galileo did and what nobody had done before was to use the telescope in such a way that the secrets of the universe were delivered to human cognition “with the certainty of sense-perception”

distinctions.distinction: In the realm of ideas there are only originality and depth without absolute objective novelty, whereas actual events and factual confirmation introduce unprecedented real-world change.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between speculative/imaginative astronomical theories prior to Galileo and the factual, sensory confirmation brought by Galileo's telescope.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Modern philosophy began with Descartes' universal doubt, which occupies a central position equivalent to the ancient Greek wonder at everything that is.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modern philosophy began with Descartes’ de omnibus dubitandum est , with doubt, but with doubt not as an inherent control of the human mind to guard against deceptions of thought and illusions of sense, not as skepticism against the morals and prejudices of men and times, not even as a critical method in scientific inquiry and philosophic speculation.

claims.claim: Cartesian doubt emerged as a response to a new reality where man-made instruments like the telescope altered the physical world view and demonstrated that reality and truth are not simply given to human senses or reason.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Cartesian doubt, in its radical and universal significance, was originally the response to a new reality, a reality no less real for its being restricted for centuries to the small and politically insignificant circle of scholars and learned men.

must_not_be_lost: Cartesian doubt as the foundational motor of modern philosophy replacing ancient wonder.
The separation of Being and Appearance as the basic assumption of modern science originating from instrument-based discovery rather than pure contemplation.
extraction.segment_function: The author examines the origins and universal scope of Cartesian doubt as a foundational pivot in modern philosophy, replacing ancient wonder with radical questioning in response to changing scientific realities and the separation of Being and Appearance.
unresolved_context: Footnote references in the source text such as 31, 31a, 32, and 33 require external bibliographic context.

claims.claim: The reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa is the most momentous and unavoidable spiritual consequence of modern discoveries.
qualifications: concomitant with the rise of Cartesian doubt and the discovery of the Archimedean point
claims.supporting_excerpt: Perhaps the most momentous of the spiritual consequences of the discoveries of the modern age and, at the same time, the only one that could not have been avoided, since it followed closely upon the discovery of the Archimedean point and the concomitant rise of Cartesian doubt, has been the reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa.

claims.claim: Modern technology originated from a non-practical search for useless knowledge rather than a pragmatic desire to improve conditions on earth.
qualifications: as a matter of historical record regarding the origins of modern technology
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is a matter of historical record that modern technology has its origins not in the evolution of those tools man had always devised for the twofold purpose of easing his labors and erecting the human artifice, but exclusively in an altogether non-practical search for useless knowledge.

must_not_be_lost: The reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa is linked directly to Cartesian doubt and the Archimedean point.
Modern technology originates from a non-practical search for useless knowledge rather than practical instincts.
extraction.segment_function: Examines the epistemological implications of modern mathematical physics, the rise of the experiment, and the historical reversal of the traditional hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa.

claims.claim: The break with contemplation in modernity was consummated by introducing the concept of process into making rather than merely reversing contemplation and action or elevating homo faber.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The break with contemplation was consummated not with the elevation of man the maker to the position formerly held by man the contemplator, but with the introduction of the concept of process into making.

claims.claim: Contemplation and fabrication share an inner affinity because beholding an idea or model is an inherent element of craftsmanship.
claims.supporting_excerpt: the philosophically much more compelling one that contemplation and fabrication ( theōria and poiēsis ) have an inner affinity and do not stand in the same unequivocal opposition to each other as contemplation and action. The decisive point of similarity, at least in Greek philosophy, was that contemplation, the beholding of something, was considered to be an inherent ele ment in fabrication as well, inasmuch as the work of the craftsman was guided by the “idea,” the model beheld by him before the fabrication process had started as well as after it had ended

extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The victory of the Christian faith in the ancient world was likely driven by its reversal of values, promising a new hope and immortality.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Historically, it is more than probable that the victory of the Christian faith in the ancient world was largely due to this reversal, which brought hope to those who knew that their world was doomed, indeed a hope beyond hope, since the new message promised an immortality they never had dared to hope for.

claims.claim: Individual life replaced the body politic as the central entity holding the position of immortality.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is precisely individual life which now came to occupy the position once held by the “life” of the body politic

must_not_be_lost: Christian reversal led to individual life becoming the highest good of man.
Political activity sank to an activity subject to necessity.
extraction.segment_function: conclusion
